sources.news_title: Australia news LIVE: Several Labor MPs want government to retain ATO credit card payments; Russia continues striking energy facilities despite ceasefire, says Zelensky
sources.text:
Australia news LIVE: ATO credit card ban solution pushed by Labor MPs; US execution live stream proposal condemned by parliamentarians; Josh Frydenberg spruiks book amid Liberal Party comeback speculation
Australia news LIVE: Deadly fire ants detected at Sydney logistics centre; Hanson-Young won’t run for Greens leadership again; Russia continues striking energy facilities despite ceasefire
Emily Kaine and James CostaUpdated October 13, 2026 — 1:15pm,first published October 13, 2026 — 6:45am
Save
You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
Hello and welcome back to our live coverage of national and international news this Tuesday, October 13. Here’s what you need to know today.
Labor’s Digital Duty of Care laws are at the forefront of political debate this week in Canberra as the Greens seek changes to the bill that would allow individuals to seek compensation for online harms. Meanwhile, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says the laws would target her party and impinge on freedom of speech.
Several Labor MPs, including some ministers, are pushing the federal government to find a permanent solution to ensure the Tax Office accepts credit cards from businesspeople with cashflow problems, three days after Treasurer Jim Chalmers stepped in to delay the Tax Office’s ban on credit card payments.
Parliamentarians have condemned the US’s potential live-streaming of an execution by firing squad of a former US Army major who killed 13 soldiers at a military base in 2009. It remains unclear if the government could legally block the livestream from being viewed in Australia.
Russia has kept up its attacks on energy assets despite US President Donald Trump claiming there were pledges from both sides to support an “energy ceasefire” in the war, Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky said.
And British comedian and actor Russell Brand appeared in a London court for the start of his trial on rape and sexual assault charges. Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault.
Latest Posts
1.15pm
Coalition attempts to move motion to reinstate credit cards for ATO bills
By James Costa
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has attempted to move a motion that would give the government the power to reverse the Australian Tax Office’s ban on the use of credit cards to pay tax bills.
On Friday, the government delayed the ATO’s decision to ban the use of credit cards to pay tax bills after the Reserve Bank’s scrapping of card surcharges was implemented. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Friday that the government wasn’t “able to direct the tax office to implement tax in a certain way”.
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson.Alex Ellinghausen
In the House of Representatives today, Wilson said “the minister for foreign affairs says that the government has no power to correct it”.
Then presto, all of a sudden, the Treasurer was able to, he was the action man, coming out and saying, ‘I’m going to extend the life of Australians being able to pay bills to the Australian Taxation Office by credit card for another 12 months’. This mysterious power they didn’t have the levers to advance the interests of Australian small business, and like presto, it suddenly appeared.
Show more
1.00pm
Taylor defends his migration cuts to business leaders
By Brittany Busch
Angus Taylor has defended his proposed cuts to migration to business leaders, who have warned of labour shortages without enough foreign arrivals.
The opposition leader told the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry that Australian migration was “well on its way” to losing its social licence.
“You know what’s business-friendly, is when we have a social licence for good immigration in this country, if we lose that … it all changes,” he said.
“The way we get it back is by shifting from what’s seen as mass migration to skilled migration.”
12.47pm
Australia out to ensure tech giants keep their social licence
By Brittany Busch
Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton has pointed to the moratorium on data centres in Texas as evidence that Australia needs to ensure tech giants maintain their social licence locally.
“Texas, home of the brave, land of the free, has introduced a moratorium on data centres,” Charlton said. “You have to lose a lot of social licence to be banned in Texas. Data centres have done that. We do not want that to happen in Australia.”
Andrew Charlton.Rohan Thomson
He said Labor’s AI standards would ensure certainty around how data centres would be powered, how they used resources and engage with communities to avoid the backlash that has been seen in the United States.
“To make sure that when they come into Australia, they come in with social licence, not to unnecessarily restrain this industry, but to put it on a stable foundation so that it can grow and deliver benefits to Australians,” Charlton said.
Advertisement
12.28pm
AI key to productivity for small businesses: Labor
By Brittany Busch
Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton has told a summit of business leaders in Canberra that artificial intelligence was a key to lifting small business productivity.
“AI offers the next opportunity to start closing that productivity gap between small businesses and big businesses,” Charlton told the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s business leaders’ summit.
“That means supporting adoption, encouraging small businesses to take up those opportunities, and in doing so, benefiting them and doing probably the biggest thing we could do to lift productivity.
“The opportunity for us is to lift the productivity of small businesses up towards the productivity of large businesses, and that has been a dream for a long time. But I think these tools make that dream a real possibility.”
12.18pm
PM says Frydenberg’s only ‘priority’ is himself
By Nick Newling
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has told his Labor colleagues that former Liberal treasurer Josh Frydenberg is only interested in himself, and has labelled the Victorian the “shadow opposition leader” following days of coverage over his forthcoming memoir.
“The shadow opposition leader has never lacked confidence in his own capacity, but when he’s had an opportunity to act, he never delivered an energy policy, and as treasurer, he never delivered the surplus,” Albanese told a caucus meeting this morning.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.Dominic Lorrimer
The prime minister said “Frydenberg’s priority has always been Josh Frydenberg”, and said he expected the former MP was “hoping people forget his record” at the upcoming Victorian state election. The leader of the Victorian Liberals, Jess Wilson, once worked as an aide to Frydenberg.
Extracts of Frydenberg’s memoir, A Grateful Son, have been circulated over the past few days, and the former MP has repeatedly appeared on television programs. Many have speculated Frydenberg is creating a launch pad for a return to federal politics after he lost to teal independent Monique Ryan at the 2022 election.
Albanese went on to criticise Opposition Leader Angus Taylor for attending the weekend’s Conservative Political Action Conference in Brisbane, and said the Liberals had “abandoned any pretense of being a centre-right party”.
The FTI Consulting estimate, prepared for the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network and seen by this masthead, is more than 500 times the roughly $1 million Telstra says it has paid in compensation.
ACCAN chief executive Carol Bennett said the telco at fault “didn’t foot the bill”. “Australian households and small businesses did,” she said.
Telstra chief executive Vicki Brady in July. Louise Kennerley
Telstra said it had not seen the research, but the figures appeared to “significantly overstate” the outage’s economic effect.
ACCAN wants senators debating the Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation bill this week to impose enforceable reliability standards on mobile networks. The Coalition says its amendments will ensure the findings of an inquiry by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, due next year, are properly considered.
Advertisement
12.07pm
Court approves notorious childcare paedophile’s extradition to NSW
By Matt Dennien
Queensland Attorney-General Deb Frecklington has told parliament that notorious childcare paedophile Ashley Paul Griffith has been approved for extradition to NSW to face further charges in the southern state.
“I do wish to take this opportunity at the first available opportunity to inform the House that ... in the last 20 minutes or so, the Magistrates Court of Queensland has determined to extradite Ashley Paul Griffith to New South Wales to, I understand, [face] around 180 charges relating to children in New South Wales,” Frecklington said.
Notorious paedophile Ashley Paul Griffith will be extradited to NSW to face almost 200 charges.Nine
“[This is] something that I have been working as attorney with the New South Wales Attorney-General Michael Daly on for several months, and the reason why I was so determined to support that application was because victims deserve … their time in court, and that’s what they will now get in New South Wales for that person”.
RBA braces for higher unemployment as it tackles inflation challenge
By Shane Wright
The Reserve Bank is preparing for unemployment to push higher in its bid to bring down inflation.
Minutes of the bank’s most recent monetary policy committee meeting, at which the official cash rate was pushed to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent, show a change in its attitude towards the jobs market.
The bank has what is described as a “dual mandate”, in that it seeks to hold inflation between 2 and 3 per cent while maintaining as many people in work as possible.
Recognising that inflation at 4 per cent remains well above its target, the minutes reveal a concession that unemployment may have to climb higher if inflation is to ease.
Show more
11.48am
Shoebridge calls AI committee a ‘Labor farce’
By Brittany Busch
Greens leader David Shoebridge has slammed the joint parliamentary committee into artificial intelligence, labelling its inquiry a “Labor farce”.
“It was made clear from the start that the government would not allow me as the Greens AI spokesperson to have a seat,” the senator said.
Greens leader David Shoebridge.Alex Ellinghausen
“Hard questions and serious challenges to US big tech was never part of their plan.”
We reported earlier that committee member David Pocock has claimed the committee’s early recommendation letter to the government had been “heavily vetted” by Anthony Albanese’s office.
Show more
Advertisement
11.24am
Frydenberg ‘popping up like an illegal smoke shop’: Joyce
By Emily Kaine
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce says Josh Frydenberg is “popping up like an illegal smoke shop” this week, and that his resurgence is “very bad for Angus Taylor’s health”.
“I watched [him] last night … I tell you, there’s another thing there’s not much to be gained from,” he told reporters outside Parliament House in Canberra this morning.
One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce.Alex Ellinghausen
Joyce said the former treasurer had his sights set on Taylor’s job.
“We know what you’re up to. You want to be the leader of the Coalition … and you’re setting the groundwork up now.”
Frydenberg did not confirm when he would contest a seat again, only that it was possible he could make a return to politics.

sources.news_title: Zelensky accuses Russia of violating proposed energy ceasefire
sources.text:
Kyiv, Oct. 12 (SANA) Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between the two countries, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, accusing Moscow of refusing to respect the proposed truce.
Trump said Sunday that the ceasefire would take effect immediately. However, Zelensky said Russia had attacked gas facilities, energy infrastructure and other sites, adding that 33 people had been injured in strikes on energy facilities across Ukraine.
“I think it was Putin’s answer to President Trump,” Zelensky told Fox News, saying Ukraine had not carried out attacks during the period.
Ukraine’s state news agency Ukrinform reported power outages in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike damaged the electricity grid. Energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine were also targeted overnight.
On Monday, Ukraine’s state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported new power cuts in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions because Russian attacks had damaged energy equipment. Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of the country to prevent further overloading of damaged infrastructure, the operator said.
Zelensky said on X that the strikes demonstrated Russia’s unwillingness to accept an energy ceasefire.
Separately, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Monday evening that a drone struck a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district of the capital. Several cars in the building’s courtyard caught fire, leaving one person dead and 11 injured, he said in a Telegram post.
When Trump first announced the proposed ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said the truce had come as news to him. He nevertheless described it as a major step toward ending the war, provided Washington ensured that Russia respected the agreement.
On Monday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine did not deserve the “respite” that a ceasefire would provide.
The attacks come amid months of reciprocal strikes by Russia and Ukraine on energy infrastructure, disrupting supplies on both sides. Moscow has described the facilities it targets as legitimate military objectives because they support Ukraine’s military operations. Zelensky, meanwhile, has said Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russian territory are intended to reduce Moscow’s ability to finance the war.
A/Dh

sources.news_title: The Kremlin relishes in the U.S.-Russia diesel deal and Trump's criticism of Zelensky
sources.text:
The Kremlin relishes in the U.S.-Russia diesel deal and Trump’s criticism of Zelensky
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
- Zelensky said Russia struck Ukrainian power and gas facilities hours after President Trump announced an energy ceasefire, while Ukraine has held off attacks on Russian energy sites.
- The Kremlin has not confirmed agreeing to the pause, and European officials voiced skepticism that Moscow would honor it as winter approaches.
- Russian attacks killed three people in the Kharkiv region and injured nine others, including children, as strikes continued across Ukraine.
KYIV, Ukraine — A deal between Moscow and Washington over exports of Russian diesel and fresh U.S. criticism of Ukraine’s leader mark important political victories for the Kremlin, reversing some of the sanctions for its full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
While the size of Russia’s diesel exports is relatively small and unlikely to significantly impact prices, the revenue will help Moscow replenish its war coffers and — more importantly — undermine efforts by Kyiv and its European allies to put up a united front against President Vladimir Putin.
Along with President Trump suggesting that Ukraine should get a new leader to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky, the developments strengthen the Kremlin’s hand at a critical junction of the war, amid relentless attacks by Russia on energy systems and other vital infrastructure.
Ahead of next month’s midterm elections, Trump blamed a spike in diesel prices on Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, even though the U.S.-led war in Iran has sent global energy prices soaring.
Mark Galeotti, a Russia expert who heads the Mayak Intelligence consultancy, described the deal that Trump announced Friday as an “astonishing birthday present” for Putin, two days after he turned 74.
While Russia’s diesel exports could be a “drop in the ocean compared with actual overall demand,” Galeotti said it was “a gift for Putin, even if a single barrel of diesel is not exported.”
That’s because “it drives another and increasingly thick wedge between Trump and Zelensky,” he said in a podcast Sunday.
Russian strikes continue despite Trump’s ‘energy truce’
Even though Trump declared Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to an “energy truce” effective immediately, Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s energy facilities, said Zelensky, who has criticized the diesel deal as a show of weakness.
Zelensky emphasized that he is open to an energy ceasefire if it includes a halt to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power grid.
Russia has not said whether it agrees to such a ceasefire, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday only that “contacts are ongoing.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov shrugged off Zelensky’s comments as an attempt “to promote his interest in a ceasefire.”
“I don’t think he deserves a respite,” Lavrov said.
Galeotti predicted that Putin is unlikely to halt attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities, which he sees as “absolutely central to his winter air war strategy.”
Russia stepped up aerial attacks on Ukraine in recent months with ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Kyiv’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors whose stockpiles have been drained by the war in Iran.
Putin has repeatedly emphasized that Moscow wants a comprehensive, long-term agreement, not a temporary halt to hostilities.
Asked to comment on Zelensky’s statement that Ukraine needs a minimum of 60 days to prepare elections, Peskov said Putin could order a ceasefire only on the day of voting.
Russia’s fuel crisis causes doubts about export capacity
In recent months, Ukraine launched successful aerial attacks that knocked out over half of Russia’s oil refining capacity, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry. The strikes caused a severe fuel crisis with long lines at gas stations, bringing the war home to millions.
Ukraine also methodically struck oil terminals at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk and targeted dozens of tankers at sea, seeking to derail Moscow’s oil exports and drain Moscow’s revenues.
Putin acknowledged the damage but noted that Moscow is capable of inflicting much bigger blows to Ukraine.
Some officials and analysts questioned whether Russia will be able to provide diesel supplies under the deal announced by Trump.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski voiced doubts about it, saying that even the Russian capital is experiencing fuel shortages.
Others say Moscow actually has a surplus of diesel, now that demand has eased following the end of the harvest season.
“Russia planned to export more diesel anyway,” said Janis Kluge, head of the Eastern Europe and Eurasia Division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs.
Still, some Russian motorists exhausted by months of waiting at gas stations were worried the new deal could leave fewer supplies for the domestic market.
“I don’t think that’s very good, because you can see what’s going on at gas stations — people are standing in line around the clock,” said Marat Salavatov, waiting to refuel at a Moscow gas station.
Russian officials sought to quell such fears, saying there will be enough supply to keep the domestic market stable.
The volume of production is able “to fully satisfy the needs of the local market while delivering the agreed amounts to the global market,” Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said in a government statement announcing the lifting of the diesel export ban that had been in place since July.
Trump’s criticism of Zelensky is seen as aiding Russia
In addition to the diesel deal, Trump unleashed biting criticism of Zelensky that marks perhaps the lowest point in their relationship since the disastrous Oval Office meeting in February 2025.
That could be even more important for the Kremlin.
Trump’s remark that it was time for a new president in Ukraine and his suggestion that Zelensky has not done enough to end the war nulltopped the news on Russian state television and was widely discussed by pro-Kremlin commentators and military bloggers.
Officials in Kyiv viewed the diesel deal and the hostile rhetoric as a political move aimed at making Zelensky a scapegoat for U.S. voters ahead of the midterms, said Oleksandr Merezhko, a lawmaker from Zelensky’s party.
“We are not happy when our ally and partner gives money to a dictator who is killing us,” Merezhko said. “By demanding that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, Trump looks as though he cares more about the Russian war machine than about the civilians Putin is killing.”
Kyiv fears that easing sanctions without meaningful concessions from Russia could weaken Washington’s leverage over the Kremlin and further diminish prospects for fair terms to end the war.
The Trump-Zelensky tensions come as Kyiv continues to rely heavily on Washington for military assistance, including Patriot systems and vital intelligence. A disruption of that support could leave Ukraine more vulnerable.
Galeotti said Trump’s comments casting Zelensky as an obstacle to peace were “benefit No. 1 for Putin.”
Trump’s move also raises questions about the European Union’s efforts to go after Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers carrying oil to global markets, he said, observing that Europe has been left in a position “where it’s obviously just regarded as a vassal region that has to accept whatever policy comes from the White House.”
The diesel deal also will boost Russia’s credentials with developing countries, helping its posture as a great global player worthy of being a partner, Galeotti said.
Tatiana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia and Eurasia Center said the move could look like a “moment of triumph” for Putin.
“He has secured an economic deal, albeit a modest one, before a peace settlement, departing from Washington’s previous position,” Stanovaya said in a commentary.
She argued that Putin will see Trump’s current stance as “creating more favorable conditions for intensifying military pressure, aimed primarily at triggering an internal political breakdown in Ukraine rather than achieving a battlefield breakthrough.”
Still, Dmitry Medvedev, who served as a placeholder president in 2008-12 to allow Putin to get around constitutional term limits, warned against excessive optimism over Trump’s comments.
“Only our guys, ballistics and Geranium (drones) make victory closer,” said Medvedev, now deputy head of Russia’s Security Council.
Samya Kullab in Kyiv, Ukraine, contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Zelensky: Putin 'Does Not Read Truth Social'
sources.text:
Zelensky: Putin 'Does Not Read Truth Social'
|                                                       By                             John Johnson                                                                                   Posted Oct 12, 2026  11:31 AM CDT                                                       | 
Volodymyr Zelensky says he's on board with the idea of a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in regard to attacks on energy facilities—but he says Russia clearly is not. "This energy ceasefire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war," he said at a security forum in Poland, per the BBC. However, Zelensky said Russia struck multiple energy facilities overnight—long after President Trump said the ceasefire was in place. "It was clear that (Vladimir) Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelensky said, per the AP. A Kremlin spokesman said he could not comment on the energy ceasefire because talks were continuing, per the Wall Street Journal.
Zelensky, who says he had no advance notice of the energy ceasefire announced by Trump, also reiterated his call for a broader 60-day ceasefire in which his nation could hold elections. But Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov appeared to rule out that possibility. "I don't think he deserves a respite," he said Monday, referring to Zelensky. Lavrov suggested that Ukraine would use any such lull to beef up its military arsenal. Trump, who struck a surprise deal to buy Russian diesel last week, signaled frustration with Zelensky over the weekend and said Ukraine should get a new president.

sources.news_title: Ukraine ready to respond if Russia ignores energy ceasefire
'Don't Kill Our Children': Zelenskyy's Stark Warning as Trump Pushes Russia-Ukraine Energy Truce
sources.text:
'Don't Kill Our Children': Zelenskyy's Stark Warning as Trump Pushes Russia-Ukraine Energy Truce
The proposal follows Donald Trump's unconfirmed claim that Russia and Ukraine had already agreed to stop targeting energy infrastructure, while strikes continued
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has offered to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries if Moscow stops bombing his country's power plants, after Donald Trump claimed both sides had already agreed an 'energy ceasefire' even as Russian attacks continued to kill civilians.
Mr Trump said on Sunday, in a post on Truth Social, that 'both parties have agreed' to stop targeting each other's energy infrastructure, adding in capitals: 'Do not break it!' He gave no details of any agreement.
Ukrainian officials said Russian forces kept hitting energy sites in Kharkiv and Kyiv within hours. The Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office said on Monday that Russian forces struck an energy facility on the outskirts of the city after the post. Mr Zelenskyy said he first heard of the supposed deal from the media.
It is the second time in a month that Mr Trump has announced such a truce. He made a similar claim on 14 September, saying both countries had agreed not to hit each other's energy systems. Neither side confirmed it, and attacks continued.
Speaking to ABC's This Week, Mr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to reciprocate. 'We are ready for energy ceasefire, not to attack energy, both sides,' he said, adding: 'Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attack your diesel.'
Russia has spent years striking Ukraine's power plants, grids and heating facilities. Kyiv has described the campaign as 'weaponising winter.' Ukraine has in turn hit Russian refineries, which Mr Trump has blamed for rising diesel prices in the United States, where he faces criticism over fuel costs weeks before the midterm elections.
Mr Trump has also suggested Ukraine should 'get a new leader who can make a deal.' Mr Zelenskyy responded that it is 'up to Ukrainians' to choose their leader. He said he would be prepared to hold elections, which are suspended under martial law, if Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day nationwide ceasefire.
Europe Challenges Trump's 'Energy Ceasefire' Claim
Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, said in Luxembourg on Monday that she would welcome any halt to attacks on Ukraine's grid before winter, but doubted Russia would comply.
'We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it,' she told reporters. She said she would prefer a ceasefire that covered more than energy, one 'that would include people not being killed'.
Ms Kallas urged EU governments to maintain military and financial support for Kyiv. She spoke after Mr Trump reportedly agreed to lift US sanctions to allow Russian diesel onto world markets.
Several European foreign ministers questioned whether the arrangement would lower prices. Estonia's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said it appeared 'much more connected to the domestic situation in the US' than to European security.
Zelenskyy Sets Terms for Energy Truce
Speaking to ABC's This Week, Mr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to reciprocate. 'We are ready for energy ceasefire, not to attack energy, both sides,' he said, adding: 'Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attack your diesel.'
Russia has spent years striking Ukraine's power plants, grids and heating facilities. Kyiv has described the campaign as 'weaponising winter.' Ukraine has in turn hit Russian refineries, which Mr Trump has blamed for rising diesel prices in the United States, where he faces criticism over fuel costs weeks before the midterm elections.
Mr Trump has also suggested Ukraine should 'get a new leader who can make a deal.' Mr Zelenskyy responded that it is 'up to Ukrainians' to choose their leader. He said he would be prepared to hold elections, which are suspended under martial law, if Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day nationwide ceasefire.
Drone Strikes Mount as Truce Talk Grows
The Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office said a Russian drone strike on Sunday evening hit the settlement of Pisochyn, killing three people and injuring nine, including children. It said the drone struck a densely populated area near apartment blocks and shops, starting a fire.
Ukraine's Air Force said it shot down or suppressed 89 of 121 Russian drones launched overnight into Monday. It reported strikes at 15 locations, with debris falling at four more.
Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the Black Sea. It also said it had attacked Ukrainian port infrastructure and a bulk carrier bound for Odesa, which it alleged was carrying military cargo. Neither side's claims could be independently verified.

sources.news_title: Zelenskyy urges U.S. to pressure Moscow to respect 'energy ceasefire' as attacks continue
Russia striking fuel reserves despite 'energy ceasefire', Zelenskyy says
sources.text:
Russia striking fuel reserves despite Trump-ordered 'energy ceasefire', Zelenskyy says
In short:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Russia is hitting Ukraine's fuel reserves despite Donald Trump's claim the countries agreed on an "energy ceasefire".
Ukrainian officials say least 12 people were wounded in several Russian attacks on Kharkiv on Monday.
What's next?
Mr Zelenskyy says that if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine "will respond".
Ukrainian officials say Russia has continued to strike Ukraine's energy facilities despite US President Donald Trump's announcement that the countries had agreed on an "energy ceasefire".
On Monday a statement from the Regional Prosecutor's Office of Kharkiv said Russian forces had attacked an energy facility on the outskirts of the city.
That came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he "welcomed" Mr Trump's announcement, but Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv.
"There were Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump," Mr Zelenskyy said.
Mr Trump's brief social media post on Sunday announcing the purported agreement to mutually cease attacks on energy sites said that the ceasefire took effect immediately.
"Do not break it!" the post said.
Mr Trump also claimed in a social media post on September 14 that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure, but offered no details on that proposal either. Nothing came of the purported agreement.
Australia is joining other nations in backing the "energy ceasefire" while urging Moscow to "end its unjustified and unprovoked invasion" of its neighbour.
"Australia supports an energy ceasefire which is respected by Russia and contributes towards a just and lasting peace, on Ukraine's terms," a Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) spokesperson said.
Local officials say least 12 people were wounded in several Russian attacks on Kharkiv on Monday morning.
Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said drones struck a high-rise building in what is Ukraine's second-largest city.
Floors seven through to nine of the building were destroyed in the attack, Mr Terekhov said, adding that there was an intense fire at the scene.
Russia has used attacks on energy facilities in order to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's invasion.
Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponising winter".
Loading
Ukraine, meanwhile, has levelled strikes against Russian energy sites such as oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory.
Such actions prompted Mr Trump to blame Mr Zelenskyy for high diesel prices in the US weeks ahead of the midterm elections.
'Stop killing our people'
Mr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to comply with Mr Trump's requests to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system. He asked Mr Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.
"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree, if they agree," Mr Zelenskyy said.
"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people. This is only fair."
Mr Zelenskyy made the comments in Poland on Monday at the opening of the Warsaw Security Forum, where government officials, military leaders and experts discussed security challenges, NATO policy and regional stability.
Mr Zelenskyy added that he was "grateful to America", but lamented that "this is Putin's answer to Trump: Russian attacks".
"It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," he said.
"This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."
Earlier, the European Union's top diplomat welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, but said she saw no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it.
"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
"Personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy."
Wires/ABC

sources.news_title: Zelenskyy says Russia has already violated Trump's 'energy ceasefire'
sources.text:
Zelenskyy addressed the Warsaw Security Forum in one of his first reactions to renewed turmoil with Washington, following Trump's surprise energy ceasefire announcement and controversial diesel deal with Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia on Monday of violating an energy ceasefire announced by Donald Trump, saying Kyiv had not even been consulted about the purported agreement and had only learned of it through the media.
"We did not know about that. We've learned that from the media as well, that the president of the United States has secured an energy ceasefire," Zelenskyy said.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelenskyy questioned whether Moscow had agreed to the proposal at all, saying he had seen neither a public endorsement from Russia nor any let-up in its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
"We have not seen that they support this ceasefire anywhere," he said, pointing to continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities.
Large parts of Kyiv were without electricity and water when Trump made his announcement, as repair crews struggled to restore power following Russian strikes. Shortly afterwards, Russia launched another targeted attack on a power plant in Kharkiv, Zelenskyy said.
"It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," he remarked, referring to Trump's social media platform.
Zelenskyy also accused Russia of striking a Ukrainian gas production facility and a petrol station overnight, while Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries.
Despite the continued attacks, he said Kyiv remained willing to observe a reciprocal halt to strikes on energy infrastructure.
"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree if they agree," he said.
Zelenskyy offered to sign formal guarantees if Washington considered them necessary, but stressed that the US would have to secure Moscow's compliance.
Trump-Putin diesel deal sparks backlash
Zelenskyy's remarks followed several days of mounting tensions with Washington, beginning on Friday when Trump announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to US and global markets, in an attempt to bring down soaring fuel prices ahead of November's US midterm elections.
The US Treasury subsequently issued a six-month licence easing sanctions on Russian diesel already loaded onto tankers, allowing deliveries until April 2027 — a sharp reversal of Washington's efforts to restrict Moscow's energy revenues.
The move drew criticism from European leaders and US lawmakers, including a bipartisan group of senators who urged Trump to reverse course, warning that the deal could provide Moscow with fresh revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
Trump, meanwhile, blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising fuel prices and demanded that Zelenskyy halt them. On Saturday, he went further, suggesting Ukraine needed a new president and accusing its wartime leader of obstructing efforts to end the war.
On Sunday, Trump announced on Truth Social that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, although neither side had publicly confirmed an agreement.
It was not the first such declaration. A similar announcement in September failed to halt the strikes.
Against this backdrop, Zelenskyy used his Warsaw address to make a pointed appeal for Washington to change course.
"We need American pressure on Russia, not sanctions relief, not concessions, but real pressure," he said.
He argued that Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries and exports were a response to Moscow's sustained campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure, and that both sides would have to halt such attacks for a ceasefire to work.
Zelenskyy offers elections if Trump secures 60-day ceasefire
Responding to Trump's renewed pressure to hold presidential elections, Zelenskyy said voting remained impossible under current security conditions, with Russian attacks now taking place around the clock.
"From a security standpoint, that's completely impossible. We have attacks day and night," he said.
He also pointed to the logistical challenges of organising a vote for more than a million Ukrainian military personnel, including those serving on the front line.
Nevertheless, Zelenskyy signalled that he was prepared to seek changes to Ukraine's legal framework if Washington could secure a comprehensive ceasefire with Moscow.
"If there is a ceasefire and if the Americans reach such an agreement with the Russians, I'm ready to engage with our Parliament and find difficult solutions," he said.
He suggested this could involve changes to legislation and even the constitution, although constitutional amendments are prohibited under martial law.
Zelenskyy then turned Trump's own diplomatic engagement with Moscow into a challenge to the US president, arguing that Washington should be able to use its influence over Putin to secure a complete halt to hostilities.
"And if we have at least a 60 day full ceasefire, then I'll be ready to work on holding elections," he said.
Zelenskyy warns of Russian hybrid attacks
Beyond the dispute with Washington, Zelenskyy warned that Ukrainian intelligence had uncovered further Russian plans to destabilise European countries.
"Our intelligence services know that Russia is planning many, many aggressive hybrid operations against Europe, against different countries, against your countries," he told the forum.
"There is no such thing as a small act of destabilisation," he added, urging European governments to remain vigilant and united.
Zelenskyy also appealed for continued military assistance, including ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets, air-defence interceptors and funding for domestic weapons and drone production.
He called for closer defence-industrial cooperation with Poland, arguing that joint production and technological partnerships could strengthen both countries' security.
The Ukrainian president also urged European leaders to prevent further delays in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations, saying progress was essential not only politically but also for the morale of Ukrainians living through another winter of war.
"Please do not allow any pauses in Ukraine's European integration," he said.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv expected to open two negotiating clusters and wanted another two opened by the end of the year.
"Our people need to feel that despite all the difficulties, Ukraine's European future is close," he said.
He concluded by urging European leaders to ensure Washington understood that an energy ceasefire, de-escalation and credible security guarantees were urgently needed in practice, rather than simply being announced on social media.
"In reality, not just on Truth Social," he said.

sources.news_title: Zelenskyy Says Strikes to Continue If Putin Rejects Energy Truce
Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s energy ceasefire as drone attacks continue
sources.text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the U.S.-brokered "energy ceasefire" but warned Monday that Kyiv would retaliate if Moscow failed to comply, as fresh Russian drone attacks targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure just hours after President Donald Trump announced the agreement.
"It is increasingly evident that Russia is unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire proposed by the United States and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our people and communities," Zelenskyy said Monday in a post on X. "Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine."
Speaking earlier in the day via video link at the Warsaw Security Forum, he said Ukraine was prepared to sign guarantees if the U.S. required them to build trust, stressing the importance of a shared understanding of the situation. "If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond," he cautioned.
"All morning today, more and more Russian jet-powered shaheds have continued to enter our skies over Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. We shoot down many of them, and if we didn't, there would clearly be even more damage to our energy infrastructure," he said.
"For now, this is Putin's answer to Trump."
It comes after Zelenskyy lamented Russia's continued drone attacks on Ukrainian energy targets on Sunday, including a strike on a power plant in Kharkiv in eastern Ukraine close to the Russian border.
Overnight, Russia attacked state-owned Ukrainian energy company Naftogaz's gas production infrastructure in the Kharkiv region, the company said. No one was injured in the strike by the jet-powered drone, which caused a fire at the facility, it added.
Naftogaz's acting CEO, Sergii Fedorenko, said that the attack had damaged critical equipment and that employees were working to repair damage as quickly as possible and prevent any risks to operations of the energy system.
Earlier on Sunday, Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" to lower fuel costs ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on social media on Sunday.
The Kremlin said Monday that contacts are ongoing on an energy ceasefire and that it would provide more information in due course, Reuters reported. It declined to comment on whether any deal would be limited to oil refineries. Russia's presidential office didn't immediately respond to a CNBC request for further information.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, ceasefires have repeatedly proved fragile. Trump has tried several times to broker an end to the war, but none have succeeded so far.
"We've been here many times before over the last 4½ years, so I don't think we should build our hopes up too much," Neil Atkinson, former head of oil at the International Energy Agency, told "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.
Deal with Russia
On Friday, Trump said he had made a deal with President Vladimir Putin in which Russia would supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to global markets.
"The reality of it is that the volumes talked about are very small," said Atkinson, who is also a visiting fellow at the National Center for Energy Analytics. "The deal that's been agreed is not really market moving in any significant way."
According to Trump, Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and then another 4 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries.
The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, welcomed an energy ceasefire but said, "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia."
"Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war," she said in a statement Saturday.
EU foreign ministers are due to meet in Luxembourg on Monday morning to discuss the Russia-Ukraine war, among other things. The EU will adopt nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, in the single largest expansion of the bloc's sanctions list since Russia started its war, Kallas said ahead of the meeting.
Oil prices turned positive after Zelenskyy's Monday comments, after trading about 1.5% lower earlier in the session.
Brent crude futures with December delivery were up 2% to $106.82 a barrel at 10:15 a.m. ET, while West Texas Intermediate futures for November ticked 1.9% higher to $93.60 per barrel.

sources.news_title: Zelensky warns of retaliation if Russia rejects energy ceasefire
sources.text:
Zelensky warns of retaliation if Russia rejects energy ceasefire
text_fields
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday warned that Kyiv would retaliate if Moscow refused to agree to an energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump over the weekend.
“If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelensky told the Warsaw Security Forum via video link.
Trump announced the proposed ceasefire without providing details, prompting uncertainty in Kyiv. Moscow has not publicly confirmed the arrangement, while Ukraine's Western allies have expressed support for the initiative.
“We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take,” Zelensky said.
Trump's announcement came two days after he declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel. The decision drew criticism from Kyiv and European allies, who warned that the move could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelensky said any halt to Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure must be matched by an end to Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities and critical infrastructure.
“If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people,” he said.
Trump has previously announced proposed truces and other arrangements on his Truth Social platform before either Russia or Ukraine confirmed them.
“An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here in reality, not just on Truth Social,” Zelensky said.

sources.news_title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine Held Fire on Russian Energy Sites Overnight, but Russia Answered Trump’s Energy Truce With More Shahed Strikes
sources.text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not attack any Russian energy facilities overnight because U.S. President Donald Trump had announced an energy truce between Ukraine and Russia. Russia, he said, kept striking Ukrainian gas stations and energy infrastructure and has effectively answered Trump with attacks. He spoke in an interview with Fox News and in remarks at the Warsaw Security Forum, UATV English reports.
“We did not attack any energy facilities in Russia last night because President Trump said there would be an energy truce between Ukraine and Russia. We didn’t attack while Russia was hitting our gas stations, our energy infrastructure and other facilities,” Zelenskyy told Fox News.
He said the signals from Moscow were unambiguous.
“I think this was Putin’s answer to President Trump. And the signals from Russia were very clear: they know nothing about an energy truce. It’s a pity, because they always find reasons not to stop this war. That is why I believe there needs to be more pressure on Russia,” he said.
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine never discloses what it plans to do next in its operations.
Warsaw Security Forum. Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s offer is clear and fair: Kyiv will observe an energy truce if Russia does the same, and it has already shown this is more than words.
“Overnight, refineries in Russia were not burning. But at midnight, a Russian jet-powered Shahed hit a gas production facility in Ukraine. There was also a Russian strike on an ordinary gas station with several drones. And repair crews are still working to eliminate the damage from yesterday’s attacks,” Zelenskyy said.
He said Russia had therefore violated the energy truce announced by Trump, and that new jet-powered Shaheds kept entering Ukrainian airspace over Kyiv and other cities throughout the morning.
“For now, this is Putin’s answer to Trump: Russian attacks. But we are waiting. We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians. We are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take,” he said.
Data centers and online bots. Zelenskyy said that after Ukraine began responding to Russian operations against its data centers, and its strikes reached Yandex data centers, many social media platforms suddenly became easier to breathe on.
“There was less hatred, less hostility and fewer provocations, because there were fewer bots. And it is quite clear where these bots came from, if they disappeared when Yandex stopped working. This proves again and again that the source of the problems is not Europe,” he said.
He said the most important thing is for people in America to see what is happening, every morning, as the day in Europe is ending.
“To see the truth,” Zelenskyy said.
The remarks come after Zelenskyy proposed a “diesel deal” with Washington, under which Ukraine would refrain from striking Russian diesel infrastructure in exchange for protection of its power grid. On Sunday, he said Russia had hit a Kyiv power plant and energy facilities in Kharkiv region after Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire.
